title: Taming the ox
hook: fifth picture: patiently, the ox is tamed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fourth picture: the ox on a rope at last, and fighting it. Your line: it pulls. Which tug did you stay with? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

This week ran like a single road. It began with Huineng: a robe no longer handed down, then meditation and wisdom as one, like a lamp and its light. Then the oxherding pictures took over. A herdsman searching. Tracks in the mud. A glimpse of the ox among green willows. Yesterday, the rope pulled tight while the ox bolted for the hills. Every step so far has been about finding or grabbing. The fifth picture is about time. Today: taming the ox.
screen: `A LAMP AND ITS LIGHT.` → `SEARCHING, TRACKS, A GLIMPSE, A ROPE.` → `NOW: TIME.`

segments.voice: First, where the trouble starts. The preface for the fifth picture, in paraphrase, says that when one thought arises, another follows right behind it. The ox wandering off isn't one big escape; it's a chain of small ones. And the preface says these things come up from the mind, not from the surroundings. The fields aren't the problem. The wandering is. Second, keep the rope close. The verse says the herdsman keeps his whip and rope near, in case the ox strays back into the dust. That's not panic. It's the plain attention of someone who has done this every day for a while. He doesn't chase the ox across the valley anymore. He notices the first step away and turns it back. Third, what changes. The verse says that, well tended, the ox grows gentle and follows him on its own, without being tied. Nothing dramatic made that happen. Not a single great insight, not one heroic effort. Just the same small returning, again and again, until returning is the ox's habit too. Fourth, why patience is the method. Yesterday's picture was grip. Today's is the long middle, where nothing much seems to happen. It's the part of any practice that doesn't make a good story: the hundredth time back to the breath, the morning you sit anyway. Looking back on this week, that's the thread. Huineng's lamp and light are one; the glimpse and the training aren't two. The ox isn't tamed by force. It's tamed by being met, patiently, every time it wanders.
screen: `ONE THOUGHT, THEN ANOTHER.` · `KEEP THE ROPE CLOSE.` · `GENTLE, IT FOLLOWS UNTIED.` · `PATIENCE IS THE METHOD.` · then, large: `TAMED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit and rest with the breath. This time, watch for the moment one thought hooks the next, the first step of the ox toward the dust. When you notice, come back gently, without a speech to yourself about wandering. Then do it again. And again. Count nothing. Score nothing. Let the returning be easy, the way a hand keeps a rope loose but near. That's the taming. The bell holds the time.
Taming the ox. The fifth oxherding picture: through patient, daily attention, the wild ox grows gentle and follows without a rope. Today's word.
Your line: tamed. Today, pick one small practice and return to it patiently, three or four times, without needing it to go well. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Zen students often describe their daily sitting with the language of the fifth oxherding picture: noticing the mind wander and returning it, over and over, as the slow work of training.

original.note: Chinese (muniu): 'herding' or 'tending the ox', the name of the fifth oxherding picture.

trapdoor: what you thought: taming means breaking the ox's will.
what it means: patient, daily tending, returning it each time it wanders, until it follows on its own.
what a scholar hears: the Chinese title is muniu, tending the ox, and the preface locates the wandering in the mind, one thought following another.

Original 牧牛 (muniu, 'herding/tending the ox'); some translations title this picture 'taming' or 'herding'. Pronunciation approximates Mandarin.
